subject: WillowTech dedicated: burst-tolerant footprint & latency cushion
messages:
From: laura.bennett@redwood.ai
To: Amit Rao <amit.rao@willowtech.ai>
Cc: ben.carter@redwood.ai, karthik.iyer@redwood.ai
Date: Tue, 18 Aug 2026 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: WillowTech capacity ask — quick sizing questions

Hi Amit,

Thanks for the time this morning. To put numbers behind the Dedicated proposal I want to confirm a couple of inputs so our sizing and latency headroom reflect WillowTech's burst profile. Current assumptions I pulled from the scoping call:

- Steady-state qps: ~40 requests/sec (inferred)
- Peak bursts: up to 600 requests/sec for short windows (30–90s) during customer-facing events
- Average tokens per request: 1.8k input + 800 output (total ~2.6k tokens)
- Target SLO: p95 inference latency <= 250ms online (end-to-end generation)
- Model variant: quantized mix of LlamaX-13B and LlamaX-7B for fallback

Attached is a quick scoping sheet (willow_scoping_sheet.xlsx) — I filled our best-guess numbers. Can you confirm the peak burst length and whether there are quiet-hour constraints we should account for (e.g., predictable nightly drops)? Also flag if procurement needs a high-level SAP-style cost breakdown to move forward.

Next steps: if you confirm, I’ll loop in Karthik and Priyom to draft a conservative dedicated footprint and headroom cushion for the pilot.

Thanks,

Laura Bennett
Sr. Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference
laura.bennett@redwood.ai
Attachment: willow_scoping_sheet.xlsx (xlsx, 38KB)
From: Amit Rao <amit.rao@willowtech.ai>
To: laura.bennett@redwood.ai
Date: Tue, 18 Aug 2026 10:03:00 -0700
Subject: Re: WillowTech capacity ask — quick sizing questions

Hi Laura — thanks, this is great. Quick clarifications:

- Peak bursts: correct on magnitude, but slightly longer windows during product launches — we can see 600–800 rps for up to 3 minutes, spikes up to 1,200 rps for ~20–30s are possible (very network-bound events).
- Tokens: the 2.6k average is accurate for our current prompt+response distribution; there is a long-tail where a subset of requests go to ~5k tokens (~5% of traffic).
- SLO: p95 <= 250ms is what our product leadership wants; p99 target is softer (~500–600ms).
- Ops: we need an option to prioritize latency over cost during launches — i.e., temporary higher-tiered model routing or reserved burst lanes.

Procurement: I’ve cc’d procurement@willowtech.ai — they will ask for a subscription-level estimate and a short mutual action plan.

Amit
VP Engineering, WillowTech
amit.rao@willowtech.ai
From: karthik.iyer@redwood.ai
To: laura.bennett@redwood.ai, ben.carter@redwood.ai
Cc: Amit Rao <amit.rao@willowtech.ai>
Date: Tue, 18 Aug 2026 11:30:00 -0700
Subject: Re: WillowTech capacity ask — quick sizing questions

Laura / Ben — I sketched a conservative tokens/sec -> GPU mapping assuming our serving runtimes and quantized LlamaX variants. Notes below (attachment: willow_latency_model_v1.csv contains the full sim):

Quoted for context:
> "Peak bursts: 600–800 rps for up to 3 minutes, spikes to 1,200 rps for 20–30s"
> "Average tokens per request ~2.6k, 5% tail to ~5k"

Assumptions used for the calc:
- LlamaX-13B quantized throughput: ~1,800 tokens/sec per A100-equivalent GPU at p95 250ms when serving with batching disabled and KV-cache warmed.
- LlamaX-7B quantized throughput: ~3,500 tokens/sec per GPU (used as fallback for cheap, latency-friendly requests).
- Average generation tokens per request considered = 800 output tokens for pacing; input costs baked in.

Sizing quick math (target p95 <= 250ms):
- For 1,200 rps spike at 2.6k tokens/request => tokens/sec = 3,120,000 tps.
- If we route 70% to 13B and 30% to 7B for quality, effective per-GPU capacity ~= (0.7*1800 + 0.3*3500) = 2,090 tps/GPU.
- GPUs required at spike = 3,120,000 / 2,090 ≈ 1,492 GPUs (worst-case, instantaneous full-fanout).

That number is intentionally super-conservative (routes all spikes to quality models). Practical mitigations:
- Burst shaping + fallback to 7B for a portion of tail traffic (reduce 13B routing to 40%) drops modeled GPU count to ~920.
- Prefix/KV caching for repeated prompts can reduce effective tps by ~10–25% depending on workload locality.
- Use of short-lived reserved burst lanes (pre-warmed nodes) sized for 3–5x steady-state with graceful degradation.

Recommendation for pilot (to present to WillowTech):
- Baseline reserved slab: 48 GPUs (predictable steady-state and small bursts).
- Pre-warmed burst pool: 320 GPUs (handles typical 3-minute bursts with fallback rules and routing priority).
- On-demand/market burst capacity for extreme 20–30s spikes (1–2k GPUs transient) with aggressive fallback config — primarily a policy and cost decision.

I attached the CSV sim and a latency vs. GPU curve. I realize the absolute numbers sound large — the important deliverable is the headroom policy: how we route, who gets priority, and safe degradation steps.

Karthik
Staff Infra Engineer, Redwood Inference
Attachment: willow_latency_model_v1.csv (csv, 64KB)

Amit — thanks for the detail, and thanks Karthik for the simulation. Two quick clarifications before we draft the mutual action plan:

1) Prioritization: WillowTech confirms you want a policy that (a) preserves p95 <= 250ms for tier-1 traffic during launches and (b) allows graceful degradation for lower-priority users. We’ll map tiers to routing policies (dedicated slab, burst pool, on-demand).
2) Tail events: we’ll model the 5% long-tail separately and show cost-vs-latency tradeoffs (keep 5% routed to 13B or steer into async fallback).

Next steps:
- Ben will follow up with a commercial sketch (subscription tiers + burst pricing).
- Karthik & Priyom will produce a short two-page headroom appendix we can attach to the MPA.
- Laura will share the HubSpot deal and a first-pass MAP doc.

HubSpot deal: https://app.hubspot.com/deals/7654321/WLW-2026-004
Doc: WILLOW_MutualActionPlan.docx (will attach in next email)

If procurement needs an SAP-style line item, say so — Ben can provision that sheet.

Laura

Looping in a compact headroom summary (raw numbers, conservative knobs):

- Steady-state slab: 48 GPUs (covers 40 rps with KV caching and normal routing).
- Burst pool (pre-warmed): 320 GPUs (handles 600–800 rps bursts with 60% routed to 7B fallback).
- Launch-mode buffer: additional 800 GPUs on-demand with strict fallback (steer 70% to 7B, 30% to 13B) — expected short-lived cost but preserves p95 for tier-1.

Headroom rationale: with the pre-warmed pool + routing, modeled p95 falls under 250ms for 95% of events; launch-mode preserves p95 for high-priority flows at higher cost. I also added a small note on token-locality: if Willow can identify repetitive request templates, caching can reduce peak load by ~15% in simulations.

I’ll draft the two-page appendix and the short bullet rollout plan (pre-warm window, healthchecks, auto-fallback triggers).

Priyom Das
SRE, Redwood Inference
